section_title: What do we know about Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. 9 He had thirty sons, as well as thirty daughters whom he gave in marriage to men outside his clan; and for his sons he brought back thirty wives from elsewhere. Ibzan judged Israel seven years. 10 Then Ibzan died, and he was buried in Bethlehem.
11 After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. 12 Then Elon the Zebulunite died, and he was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

13 After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel. 14 He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years. 15 Then Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, died, and he was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

context_lines: Three brief notices carry the account forward after Jephthah. Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel for seven years. His thirty sons and thirty daughters marry outside their clan, connecting his large household with others. Outside the clan does not itself mean outside Israel.

Elon of Zebulun judges for ten years and is buried at Aijalon in Zebulun. Abdon of Pirathon follows for eight years. His household includes forty sons and thirty grandsons who ride seventy donkeys. He is buried in Pirathon, in Ephraim’s territory.

The account gives lengths of service, family details for two of the men, and burial places. It records no major battle or detailed evaluation of their conduct. Elon’s children are not mentioned. These notices preserve their place in Israel’s story without giving us enough to reconstruct each man’s private life or motives.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/12.htm) reads these quiet accounts as a reminder of the value of useful, peaceable lives that leave fewer dramatic events to recount. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-judges/) draws attention to the contrast between Ibzan’s many children marrying and Jephthah’s only daughter remaining unmarried. The differences between the households are noted without treating family size alone as proof of either faithfulness or corruption.
